Will your gums heal after quitting nicotine pouches?

Partly. Irritation where the pouch sat can heal after you stop. Gums that have pulled back usually don't grow back on their own. Here is what the sources say, and where they are still unsure.

Short answer. Sore, red or irritated gums and changes in the lining of your mouth can go back to normal after you quit. With tobacco snus this usually takes a few weeks. With nicotine pouches it can take months, up to a year. Gum recession, where the gum has pulled back from the tooth, does not go away even if you quit.

What pouches and snus do to your mouth

Norway's health service Helsenorge describes two kinds of changes where you keep snus:

  • Changes in the lining of the mouth: white or red patches, irritation and soreness under the lip.
  • Gum recession: the gum pulls back, so more of the tooth neck shows and the tooth wears faster.

Nicotine pouches (white snus) contain no tobacco or very little, but they still contain nicotine and can irritate the gums and damage the mouth. Even nicotine-free pouches can irritate teeth, gums and the lining of the mouth, depending on what's in them.

What can heal

Helsenorge says changes in the lining of the mouth can go back once you stop. How long it takes seems to depend on the product:

  • Tobacco snus: gums usually recover within a few weeks of quitting.
  • Nicotine pouches: dentists at the University of Gothenburg see more painful, red gum changes, thinning of the lining, sores and strong inflammation. After stopping, this damage can last several months, up to a year.

How sure is this? The Gothenburg findings come from an ongoing study of about 40 patients who already had problems from nicotine pouches, reported in a university news release in 2025. It will run for at least five years, and full results are not published yet. So we know damage from pouches can heal slowly, but not how often it heals quickly.

What usually doesn't heal

Gum recession. Helsenorge is clear that it doesn't go away even if you stop using snus. Quitting removes what was irritating that spot, and a dentist can tell you whether anything else is needed.

When to see a dentist

  • You notice a white or red patch, a sore or a change in the lining of your mouth.
  • Your gums bleed, hurt or look like they're pulling back where you keep the pouch.
  • Something hasn't improved a few weeks after you quit.

Helsenorge advises seeing a dentist or doctor if you notice changes in the lining of your mouth. The Gothenburg specialist dentist Gita Gale advises stopping right away if you get problems from nicotine pouches.

Questions people ask

Do gums grow back after quitting snus or Zyn?

Receded gums don't grow back on their own. Irritated, inflamed gums can heal.

How long until my gums feel normal?

After tobacco snus, usually a few weeks. After nicotine pouches, it can take months. If it hasn't improved, see a dentist.

Is it safer to switch sides or move the pouch around?

We haven't found a reliable source on this. What the sources agree on is that stopping is what lets the mouth heal.

Sources

  1. Helsenorge: Snus – helseskader, Norwegian Directorate of Health, updated 18 January 2023.
  2. University of Gothenburg: Long-term inflammation raises questions about white snus, 24 March 2025.
